item.title: Woman Who Says She Was Raped at Cornell Sends Message to Faculty Senate
item.description:
The former student who accused seven men of sexual assault in a lawsuit that has rocked Cornell University wrote in a letter to faculty leaders last week that she felt “unsupported” and “disbelieved” by the school’s president, Michael Kotlikoff.

In a two-page letter to the faculty senate, the former student, known as Jane Doe, said she had wanted to share a “secondhand account” as the senate considers a rare vote of no-confidence in Dr. Kotlikoff’s administration. The letter described a comment she said he had made in a meeting with students and administrators shortly after she alleged she had been raped at a fraternity house.

His “initial response,” she wrote, “was along the lines of, ‘Why did she wait so long to report it?’”

The alleged assault occurred on Oct. 19 and 20, 2024. She went to the campus police about three weeks later, on Nov. 8.

The former student wrote in a letter to faculty leaders that her experience “diminished her confidence” in the administration’s ability to take her allegations seriously.

A Cornell spokeswoman said that while Dr. Kotlikoff had made a similar comment at the January 2025 meeting, the “secondhand account” was incorrect and the words had not been directed at the former student.

“The question ‘Why did it take so long for the assault to be reported?’ was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell’s anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024,” the university said in a statement. “He was not questioning Jane Doe’s reporting.”

The former student, now 22, stopped short of telling the faculty senate how it should vote in her letter, but she said that Dr. Kotlikoff’s words, as told to her, had shaken her trust in Cornell.

“It diminished my confidence in the administration’s ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school,” she wrote.

Her letter, obtained by The New York Times and authenticated by her lawyer, was dated Oct. 14, 2026, two weeks before the faculty senate is scheduled to begin its vote. The letter shows how the woman, who dropped out of Cornell after the alleged assault, is actively trying to weigh in on the roiling debate around her claims.

“She believed that this was important information that the faculty should know when considering what steps to take” in relation to Dr. Kotlikoff, said Thomas P. Giuffra, her lawyer.

While the faculty senate has no power to remove officials, a no-confidence vote would be a strong rebuke of Dr. Kotlikoff, who has had the support of Cornell’s powerful board of trustees in the face of some calls for his resignation. The senate will meet to debate the no-confidence resolution on Oct. 28, with voting continuing for several days after.

Mr. Giuffra sent the letter on behalf of Jane Doe to Samuel Mayer Nelson, the speaker of the faculty senate, and Chris B. Schaffer, the dean of faculty. It was unclear how many of the approximately 135 members of the faculty senate had seen the letter by Tuesday afternoon.

Early Tuesday morning, Dr. Schaffer sent an email to faculty senators acknowledging that he had received Jane Doe’s letter, and relaying the administration’s rebuttal to it. He described the contents of her letter broadly, and did not include it as an attachment.

“The dean of faculty office does not have the investigatory capacity to properly follow up on private communications of this kind, nor is this the role of the office,” he wrote to the senators, adding that the rebuttal from the administration had come from a “contemporaneous account of the meeting from a university official who was present.”

Dr. Schaffer wrote that he had forwarded the letter to Cornell’s lawyers, as well as the special investigative team, headed by Sally Yates, a former deputy attorney general, that Cornell had appointed to further examine the case and the university’s broader response to sexual assault issues.

Ariana Kim, a co-sponsor of the faculty no-confidence resolution, said she was concerned that the faculty dean still had not shared Jane Doe’s letter with her or the wider senate nearly a week after receiving it.

“It echoes and cements the feelings many of us are already having, about Cornell wanting to keep things as quiet as possible,” she said.

Cornell has faced intense criticism for its handling of the former student’s allegations in the weeks since she filed a lawsuit against the university; the Chi Phi fraternity and seven of its former brothers; and her sorority, Delta Delta Delta.

In the lawsuit, Jane Doe claims she was given drugs and gang raped over several hours in the Chi Phi fraternity house. All of the men have denied wrongdoing and none have been charged with a crime.

When the former student reported her allegations to the campus police a few weeks later, a Title IX investigation was triggered.

The meeting the former student referred to in her letter took place in January 2025 and included representatives of many of Cornell’s sororities as well as Dr. Kotlikoff and at least one other administrator, according to a person with direct knowledge of the meeting who spoke on the condition of anonymity to reveal details of a private meeting.

According to a Cornell official familiar with the matter, the conversation took place at a meet-and-greet for Dr. Kotlikoff as he was getting to know student groups during his time as interim president. The official Cornell account comes from contemporaneous notes from the meeting taken by the other administrator.

In the letter, the former student recounts the exchange that she said she was told happened between Dr. Kotlikoff and the president of her sorority. She wrote that her sorority sister relayed the conversation to her “with concern.”

“She interpreted his question as an expression of doubt in the veracity of my story,” Jane Doe said in the letter.

The sorority president said other faculty or staff members had heard the conversation, according to the letter, and that “at least one of them appeared distressed” by the president’s comment.

“When the then-Tri Delta president relayed this conversation to me, I felt unsupported and disbelieved by President Kotlikoff,” the former student wrote. “I am sharing this account now because, to my knowledge, only a few individuals are aware of the conversation; I do not know if you or other members of the faculty senate are among them.”

She added, “I would not want to withhold something potentially pertinent, only for senate members to later discover that information relevant to their deliberations had not been made available to them.”

The former president of the Cornell chapter of Tri Delta declined to comment.

Dr. Kotlikoff has said he was not aware of the details of the former student’s case after her initial report, but has stressed that he took its claims of drug and alcohol fueled abuse seriously enough to create a presidential task force on campus sexual assault in February 2025.

Cornell ultimately barred the fraternity from campus, expelled two of the accused men and suspended two others. The other three men accused by the former undergraduate received lighter punishments.

At about noon on Tuesday, Ms. Yates sent an email to students, faculty members and alumni of Cornell to reassure them of her independence as she undertook her inquiry and to ask for any relevant information they might have to share.

“We also know that a lot of people are counting on us — counting on us to speak the truth; counting on us to be fair; counting on us to get this right,” she wrote. “We will devote everything we have to live up to those expectations.”

She said that the board of trustees had pledged to provide her team with full autonomy and that the board planned to publicly release the results of her review and recommendations.

Hurubie Meko and Andrea Barnes contributed reporting.

item.title: College Football Superlatives
item.description:
Good morning! It’s already the midway point of the college football season. My alma mater did not have a football team, as I’ve probably mentioned, so all this is a little new to me.

I am getting a bit of a crash course from my colleagues at The Athletic, who are handing out midseason superlatives. Miami was named the best team; James Madison was deemed the best team from a non-Power 4 conference; Jeremiah Smith, a wide receiver for Ohio State, was named the best player; and Oregon State’s Jesse Legree was called “college football’s biggest surprise.”

Read more superlatives here, and see The Athletic’s ranking of every team.

Already over football? It’s almost basketball season. Florida was at the top of The Associated Press’s preseason poll, followed by Duke, Illinois and Connecticut.

We’re also covering:

Origins of life

The Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show

Deep fried eggs

What you need to know to be the smartest person in class today.

1. France extended its curfews. The country’s prime minister said the measures helped keep the calm overnight after days of rioting and looting.

2. Mahmoud Khalil appealed to the Supreme Court to stop his deportation. Khalil had recently graduated from Columbia University when he was arrested by ICE and became the face of the Trump administration’s crackdown on pro-Palestinian demonstrations.

3. Residents of Alberta voted to remain a part of Canada. They rejected a campaign to try to separate the oil-rich province from the rest of the country. Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the result.

4. Christiane Amanpour said she was leaving CNN. Amanpour, one of the most famous names in broadcast news, is stepping down next year. She started at CNN in 1983.

5. How did life arise on Earth? Three moments may offer some clues. I’m trying not to get too existential.

What you’re eating.

Avocado toast may be a millennial delicacy, but the fruit is full of nutrients. Here’s what Amelia Kingsley, 19, a chemistry major at Yale, does with them:

What are you eating? A whole avocado.

Where? In the library, in class or in the dining hall.

Her hack: I keep a stash of whole avocados in my dorm. In the morning I put one in a jar in my bag so it doesn’t get crushed, adding it to dining hall salads for extra nutrients and healthy fats.

Submit your meals to Dining Hall.

The City University of New York raised $312 million in donations during the 2026 fiscal year. My colleague James Barron talked to the chancellor to learn more.

David Sabatini, a prominent scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who was forced out of his job over sexual harassment allegations, won a defamation case against his accuser, along with a $6 million award.

The vibes were high during Cornell University’s homecoming tailgate, but as nighttime came around, the effects of the party ban led to a more subdued scene.

The former Cornell student who accused seven men of sexual assault in a lawsuit sent a letter to faculty leaders last week, saying that she felt “unsupported” and “disbelieved” by the school’s president. Read the letter.

Kylie Jenner walked the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. She wore the Fantasy Bra, a $50 million piece with thousands of diamonds on it.

Can you guess which snack has Copenhagen in a chokehold? It’s literally sliced cheese on bread with butter, known locally as a bolle med ost (bun with cheese), shortened to BMO. The city’s top bakeries are striving to perfect the snack.

Get dumped by A.I. on reality TV. Three celebrities dated A.I. avatars on a South Korean show called “My A.I. Partner: Strange Love.” One contestant went on a pool date with one, slept next to another and was dumped by a third.

Do this to get ahead.

Fry an egg. If you can’t decide between sunny side up or over easy, how about deep frying it? Egg katsu is blowing up online. Try this recipe.

Play a board game. It could be a great way to bond (or start beef) with your friends. Here are the best ones.

Eat some seaweed. It’s great for your gut, is a complete source of protein and has some vitamins, too. Now I’m craving seaweed salad!

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A. See you tomorrow!

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com

The editor of Extra Credit is Talya Minsberg. Scott Nelson was our photo editor.

item.title: A Matter of Values, at Cornell and Beyond
item.description:
To the Editor:

Re “Inside the Crisis Response at Cornell’s Chi Phi House” (front page, Oct. 12):

What does it take for a room full of educated young men to realize that a woman could be in danger? A Snapchat message advertising access to her body wasn’t enough.

The New York Times’s reporting on Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity highlights a much bigger issue. One fraternity brother entered the room after seeing the message and later told investigators that everything seemed normal. He also admitted to “bantering” about it beforehand in the group chat. What is particularly disturbing is how casually the situation was treated.

This is not just a Cornell problem. It reflects a culture in which degrading women is brushed off as a joke, sexual violence is not taken seriously enough and fitting in with a group becomes more important than doing the right thing.

As a woman at a university, I’ve constantly been reminded of the precautions I should take to protect myself. Don’t drink too much. Don’t walk alone. Watch your surroundings. But why aren’t we putting that same energy into addressing the attitudes and behaviors that make women feel unsafe in the first place? We need to stop treating sexual violence as something women are responsible for preventing and start questioning how we are raising young men.

Real change starts long before college, with teaching boys to respect women, recognize harmful behavior and hold one another accountable. This isn’t just a problem for universities to solve. It’s a problem with the values and attitudes our society continues to normalize.

Sarah GalatasAtlantaThe writer is a graduate student of social work at the University of Georgia.

To the Editor:

Just because fraternity members call each other “brothers” does not mean that The New York Times has to do the same in its reporting. With numerous reports of sexual assaults at fraternities on campuses — more than in non-Greek spaces — it is abundantly clear that many fraternity members across the country do not treat women well.

Jane Doe was a sorority member, which in Greek life meant she was a sister to the brothers at Chi Phi. What brother would participate in such an abusive group chat about his sister? The undisputed behavior of the “brothers” at Chi Phi at Cornell was beastly and ugly, even if not found to be criminal. In no definition of the word did these men treat Jane Doe as their sister.

Ruth DellTiburon, Calif.

To the Editor:

Re “Want to Address Sexual Assault? Make Fraternities Coed,” by Michael S. Roth, the president of Wesleyan University (Opinion guest essay, Oct. 17):

I was particularly struck by Dr. Roth’s observation that at Wesleyan people who see someone in a vulnerable position are now more likely to speak up. That change may be as important as any institutional reform he describes.

For many years, as an artist and the founding president of the nonprofit Have Art: Will Travel!, working with educators and curriculum scholars, I have been exploring a related question: Can we teach people to move from being bystanders to becoming upstanders?

Through art exhibitions, student discussions and a yearly $5,000 Upstander Award recognizing people who intervene on behalf of others, I have seen how important it is not merely to condemn harmful behavior but also to make intervention itself visible, discussable and valued.

Dr. Roth’s experience suggests that upstander behavior is not simply a quality some courageous individuals happen to possess. Institutions can help create cultures in which people feel both empowered and responsible to act.

Universities should ask not only how they can prevent people from causing harm, but also how they can prepare the rest of us to refuse to stand silently by when harm occurs.

Linda SteinNew York

To the Editor:

Re “Where Was the Courage at Cornell?,” by David French (column, Oct. 14):

Debates rage about what causes events similar to what happened at Cornell. Mr. French got it right; it’s what didn’t happen at Cornell that matters.

Even young men whose brains are said not to be fully formed until around age 25 can be challenged and encouraged by their college to do the right thing when bad things happen. As Mr. French points out, the courage and decency to say “Stop” wasn’t present, which he ascribes to a lack of virtue.

In ancient Athens, virtue was a constant theme of discussion in the agora of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle. We need more of that kind of discussion at our colleges — perhaps in a class of ethics, which I suggest ought to be an undergraduate course requirement. Such a class should link discussion about personal and group responsibility, care, respect, diligence and even brotherly love.

Conrad EbersteinGlen Allen, Va.

To the Editor:

Re “Avalanche of G.O.P. Cash Keeps the Party Competitive Despite Its Problems” (news article, nytimes.com, Oct. 16):

Millions of voters can outvote billions of dollars of American oligarchs’ propaganda. Let’s hope we do.

Martin S. KaplanNew York
